Confusion
kon-fū'zhun
n. (disorder, shame; rendering Hebrew bosheth and tohu, Greek akatastasia)
From the Latin confusio, from confundo, to pour together. Hebrew bosheth is shame, and tohu is formlessness — the word describing the earth before the third day — so biblical confusion is both disorder and the disgrace attending it.

Biblical Definition

Confusion in Scripture is disorder, and disorder is presented as contrary to God's nature rather than merely inconvenient. Its origin as a proper name is Babel: “Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9) — a judgment on a united humanity building a tower to make itself a name, and the confusion of tongues is the scattering of that project. Paul makes the theological principle explicit and applies it to worship: “God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1 Corinthians 14:33). The argument is from the divine character to the shape of a service, which is why order in the assembly is a matter of obedience and not preference. James names the source of confusion in a congregation with uncomfortable precision: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16) — not doctrinal error in that instance but envy, the sin nobody confesses. The word also carries the older sense of shame, in which the Psalmist prays to be spared: “In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion” (Psalm 71:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Disorder, and also shame. Babel is confusion as judgment; Paul argues from God's character that he is not the author of confusion but of peace; James traces it in a church to envy and strife.

expand to see more

CONFUSION, n. [L. confusio, from confundo, to pour together.] In a general sense, a mixture of several things promiscuously; hence, disorder; irregularity.

2. Tumult; want of order in society; as, a city in confusion.

3. Abashment; shame; as, he was put to confusion before them all.

4. Astonishment; agitation; distraction of mind.

5. In Scripture, God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, 1 Cor. 14; the name of it called Babel, Gen. 11.

Key Scripture

Genesis 11:9 — "Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth. Babel: that is, Confusion"

1 Corinthians 14:33 — "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints."

James 3:16 — "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work."

Psalm 71:1 — "In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion."

Modern Corruption

Disorder in worship is defended as spiritual liberty, and disorder in a church is blamed on personalities or structures. Paul grounds order in the character of God, and James traces confusion to envy and strife.

expand to see more

The claim that structured worship quenches the Spirit runs directly into 1 Corinthians 14, the chapter most concerned with the extraordinary gifts, which regulates them and concludes that all things be done decently and in order. Paul's reason is not pragmatic. He says God is not the author of confusion but of peace, so a disorderly assembly misrepresents the God it gathers to worship. The regulative principle follows from this: worship is ordered by what God has commanded, because the God who commands is himself a God of peace.

James 3:16 supplies the harder diagnosis, and it is one congregations resist. When a church falls into confusion, the causes offered are usually structural or personal — poor communication, difficult members, unclear leadership. James names envying and strife, and adds every evil work, meaning confusion is not only a symptom but a doorway. The principle to recover is that the remedy runs through repentance rather than reorganisation, and the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bosheth is shame, tohu is formlessness or vanity, and balal is to mingle or confound — the verb behind the name Babel. Greek akatastasia is instability, tumult, or confusion.

expand to see more

Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, to confound; the verb from which Babel is named.

Hebrew bosheth (H1322) — shame, confusion of face; the older English sense of the word.

Hebrew tohu (H8414) — formlessness, waste, vanity; the earth was without form, Genesis 1:2.

Greek akatastasia (G181) — instability, disorder, tumult; the word in 1 Corinthians 14:33.

Greek eirene (G1515) — peace; what God is the author of instead of confusion.

Usage

"Of the judgment at Babel: because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9)."

"Of God's character governing worship: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace (1 Corinthians 14:33)."

"Of its source in a congregation: where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work (James 3:16)."
